Delayed peripheral facial palsy in the stapes surgery is a serious complication that can occur due to reactivation of Herpes Simplex Virus 1 (HSV-1) within the geniculate ganglion. This condition can lead to permanent damage or nerve function impairment.

Prevention of delayed peripheral facial palsy requires an adequate acyclovir therapy following stapes surgery. The American Academy of Otolaryngology recommends that patients with a history of herpes labialis be provided with prophylactic treatment to prevent reactivation and subsequent infection in the geniculate ganglion during or after stapes surgery.

It is essential for surgeons and healthcare providers to closely monitor patients who have undergone stapes surgery, especially those with a history of HSV-1 infections, to detect any potential reactivation. Prompt treatment with acyclovir can help prevent or minimize the severity of delayed peripheral facial palsy.

In summary, delayed peripheral facial palsy in the stapes surgery is likely caused by reactivation of latent HSV-1 within the geniculate ganglion and can be prevented by providing adequate preoperative acyclovir therapy.
